member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.Application.TargetFrameRate

Frames per second the loop is paced to, whether that loop is the editor's, a standalone game's or a headless server's. Zero or less runs unlimited, which is what a game starts at until its own code says otherwise. This is a ceiling, so with on the lower of the two wins.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.AssetImporting.LightmapUVGenerator
member.summary:
Generates a second UV set (UV2) suitable for lightmapping by running Prowl.Unwrapper over a mesh and baking the resulting atlas UVs into .
The unwrapper produces per-corner UVs (one per triangle corner) with seams between charts, whereas a Mesh stores per-vertex attributes. So we split vertices wherever corners that share an original vertex disagree on their lightmap UV, duplicating every other attribute (position, normal, uv, tangent, color, bone data) onto the new vertices. The index buffer keeps the same length and triangle order, so existing submesh ranges stay valid.

member.summary: Unwrap and write the result into its UV2 channel. Best-effort: on failure (degenerate geometry, etc.) it logs a warning and leaves the mesh unchanged.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.AssetImporting.IModelTextureResolver
member.summary:
Strategy for turning a model's texture references into textures during import. Invoked once per distinct texture the model references (the caller caches and reuses the result across every material slot that references the same texture).
The default (used when nothing else is supplied) decodes and GPU-uploads immediately - correct for a direct runtime load with no separate asset-tracking step to hand off to. The editor supplies its own implementation that never decodes another asset's pixel data itself: an externally referenced texture is resolved purely by path, against the asset database's existing GUID for that file, and an embedded texture is registered as a proper sub-asset for the asset database to own and cache - so importing a model never grows or duplicates the pixel data of anything else.

member.returns: The texture, or null if it can't/shouldn't be resolved - the caller falls back to the material slot's built-in default texture (Grid/Normal/Surface/Emission).
member.param: Whether materials sample it as colour, so the GPU decodes it; normal, surface and occlusion maps are data.

member.name: E:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.DeviceClosing
member.summary: Raised immediately before the device is closed, while everything built from it is still valid. Release native objects here rather than after the fact: once the context is gone, so is the node graph they are attached to, and uninitializing them then is a use after free.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.ToAudioSpace(Prowl.Vector.Float3)
member.summary: Converts a world position, direction or velocity into the space the audio engine works in.
member.remarks: Prowl is left handed with +Z forward, the audio engine is right handed with -Z forward, so the two disagree by a mirror on one axis. Mirroring the vectors that cross the boundary is what gets all three axes right. Mirroring one of the listener's basis vectors instead (negating its world up, say) also lines left and right back up, but it does it by flipping the handedness of the basis, which leaves vertical inverted.

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.Suspended
member.summary: Stops the device without closing it, freezing everything that is playing exactly where it is. Set it for a pause menu, clear it to pick every voice up where it left off.
member.remarks:
Silencing the master volume instead would leave the mix running, so a game coming back from a pause would find its music part way past where it stopped.
Play mode being paused suspends the device too, and the two are tracked apart, so the editor resuming cannot clear a suspension the game asked for or the other way round.

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.SuspendedByPause
member.summary: Suspends the device for as long as play mode is paused. Driven by the game loop, which is why this is not the one game code sets: that is .

member.summary: Initializes MiniAudioEx. Call this once at the start of your application.
member.param: The sample rate to use. Typical sampling rates are 44100 and 48000.
The number of channels to use. For most purposes 2 is the best choice (stereo audio).
Buffer size for audio processing. This value is a 'hint' so in practice it may be different than what you passed.
If left null, a default device is used.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.Restart(System.UInt32,System.UInt32,System.UInt32,Prowl.Runtime.Audio.DeviceInfo)
member.summary: Reopens a running device with a different format or on a different output. Does nothing if the settings already match, and nothing at all if no device is open. Opening the first one is 's job.
member.remarks:
Everything the old device owned is invalid afterwards, which is what exists to tell the rest of the engine. Decoded clip data is not device owned and survives untouched.
The no device case is not an oversight. Project settings are applied from paths that never wanted audio, headless builds and dedicated servers among them, and reopening had no way to tell those apart from a real format change.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.Reopen
member.summary: Closes the device and opens it again on the same settings. For picking a device back up after it has stopped underneath the engine, which will not do because nothing about the settings has changed.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.FindDevice(System.String,System.Int32)
member.summary: Finds a playback device by the name it reports, falling back to a position in the list. Null if neither finds one.
member.remarks: Names are what survive between two runs. An index is a position in whatever the backend enumerated this time, so plugging in a headset renumbers the devices after it and a setting saved as an index quietly comes back pointing at a different output.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.RecoverFromDeviceLoss
member.summary: Notices a device that has stopped without being asked to and opens it again.
member.remarks:
A device can go on its own: the output it was using is unplugged, the driver resets, the system moves the default elsewhere. miniaudio follows the system default on its own for a device opened without naming one, so this is the backstop for the cases where it cannot, and those used to be the rest of the session in silence with nothing logged.
One attempt, then it stays quiet. A machine with no working output would otherwise reopen a device it cannot have once a frame, and every failure logs.

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.PeriodSizeInFrames

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.UniqueKeyFlag
member.summary: A key with this bit set belongs to a clip that asked for a buffer of its own. Content hashes give the bit up so the two spaces cannot meet, and a clip that asked not to share cannot be handed someone else's buffer because a hash happened to equal a counter.

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.ContentKeyMask
member.summary: Masks a content hash down to the space shared buffers are keyed in.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.AcquireUniqueClipHandle(System.Byte[],System.Int32,System.UInt64@)
member.summary: Allocates a buffer that is never shared and returns the key it is held under, or IntPtr.Zero if the allocation failed. Released the same way a shared one is.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.AcquireClipHandle(System.UInt64,System.Byte[],System.Int32)
member.summary: Takes a reference on the shared native buffer for , allocating and filling it from if this is the first caller to ask for it. Release it with . Returns IntPtr.Zero if the allocation failed.
member.remarks: Lookup and insert are one operation on purpose. Splitting them let two clips with identical data both miss the lookup and both allocate, and it let a caller adopt an existing buffer while forgetting to count the reference, which freed the buffer out from under the other holder.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.RetainClipHandle(System.UInt64)
member.summary: Takes another reference on a buffer that is already cached, without needing the bytes it was built from. Returns false when nothing is cached under .
member.remarks: This is what lets a buffer outlive the that loaded it. Playback hands the raw pointer to the native decoder, which reads it on the audio thread for as long as the voice sounds, and the clip is free to be disposed in the meantime: an asset reimport does exactly that, and so does a clip nothing kept a reference to being collected. Freeing the buffer while a voice is reading it is a use after free with no useful stack.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.GetClipRefCount(System.UInt64)
member.summary: How many clips currently hold the shared buffer for this hash, 0 if it is not cached.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioContext.ReleaseClipHandle(System.UInt64)
member.summary: Drops one reference on a shared buffer, freeing it once the last holder lets go.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioBuffer
member.summary: Hands the most recent block of audio from the audio thread to the game thread, for meters, scopes and spectrum displays.
member.remarks:
One writer and one reader, and the writer never waits. Both used to take the same lock, which meant the audio thread could block behind the game thread copying the whole buffer out: the game thread stalling is a slow frame, the audio thread stalling is an audible dropout.
Instead the writer bumps a counter either side of the copy, odd while it is mid-write. The reader takes the counter, copies, and takes it again: unchanged and even means it saw a whole block, and anything else means the writer overtook it, so it retries a few times and then reports nothing new. Missing an occasional block is invisible in a visualiser, which is all this feeds.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioBuffer.Write(Prowl.Runtime.Audio.Native.NativeArray{System.Single})
member.summary: Copies as much of as fits and returns how much that was. Anything past the capacity is dropped rather than written past the end of the array, which is what happened when the destination was sized from the source and so bounds-checked itself.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioBuffer.Read(System.Single[]@)
member.summary: Copies the samples written by the last into , growing it to hold them if it is too small, and returns how many are valid. Returns 0 when the writer kept overtaking the read, meaning there is nothing consistent to show.

member.summary: A named bus that audio is routed through on its way to the device, carrying a volume and a mute for everything feeding it.
member.remarks: Groups live inside an and are referenced by an . Each one owns a native sound group whose output is attached to its parent's, so a volume set on a parent scales every descendant. The native side is built on demand and thrown away when the device closes, so the asset stays pure data.

member.summary: Hears this bus on its own. Deliberately not saved: soloing is something you do while listening to a mix, not a property of it, and a project that opened with a bus soloed would be a mystery.
member.remarks: While anything is soloed, a bus sounds only if it is the soloed one, is inside it, or is on the path it takes to the output. That last part is what makes soloing a child audible at all: every bus between it and the master has to keep passing audio.

member.summary: Base class for effects in an 's processing chain.
member.remarks:
Parameters belong in serialized fields so the effect can be authored in the inspector and saved with the scene. Anything derived from the audio format belongs in , which runs once the sample rate and channel count are known, rather than in a constructor that makes the caller pass in values the engine already has.
runs on the audio thread. It must not allocate, block, or take a lock: a garbage collection or a contended lock there is an audible dropout, not a slow frame.

member.remarks: Tested per block rather than filtered out when the chain is built, so toggling this from gameplay works without anything having to republish the chain afterwards. The audio thread may read a value one block stale, which is inaudible, and the alternative was a toggle that only worked from the inspector.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.Effects.AudioEffectChain
member.summary: Runs an ordered set of effects over one block of audio, on behalf of an or an .
member.remarks:
The chain works in buffers it owns rather than passing the node graph's own input and output back and forth. Doing that only worked while the two frame counts happened to be equal: the copy in one direction needs the input to fit the output and the copy back needs the opposite, so any block where the graph handed over different counts threw. It also meant writing into the upstream node's output buffer, which is not ours to modify.
Everything here runs on the audio thread. It allocates only when the block size grows past what it has already seen, and never blocks.

member.summary: Runs every effect over one block and writes the result to . Returns how many frames were written, which is what the caller should report to the graph.
member.remarks: With no effect changing the count that is the smaller of the two frame counts, because a one to one chain cannot produce more audio than it was given. Reporting the requested count instead would mean claiming frames that were never written.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.Effects.DelayEffect
member.summary: Fixed delay line with optional feedback, for slapback and echo.
member.remarks: An insert, so the signal that goes in comes back out with the repeats added to it. It used to replace the input with the contents of the delay line instead, which meant dropping a delay on a source removed the sound and left only a copy of it arriving a quarter of a second later.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.Audio.Effects.DelayEffect.DelayLine
member.summary: The buffer and the geometry that describes it, as one thing.
member.remarks: These three have to agree. Held as separate fields, resizing wrote the new frame count and then swapped the array, so a block landing between the two indexed the old, shorter buffer with the new, larger count and ran off the end of it. Swapping one reference instead means the audio thread reads a set that was never half updated.

member.summary: Playback position, counted in the frames the device runs at.
member.remarks:
This is the engine's own read position, so it advances at the rate the device was opened at whatever rate the clip was authored at. That is not the unit is in, so the two do not belong in one expression. is what compares them.
It also keeps counting across a loop rather than starting over, so on a looping source it is how long the source has been sounding for. is where in the clip it currently is.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.AudioSource.EnsureEffectNode
member.summary: Builds the node that runs this source's chain, if anything needs one and there is not one already.
member.remarks:
Built on demand rather than for every source. The node is a managed callback across the native boundary for every block, plus a copy through the chain and another into the capture buffer, and most sources in a scene have no effects and nobody listening. That was being paid per source per block on the audio thread to move audio from one buffer to an identical one.
Kept once built. Taking it back out would mean detaching the graph under a sounding voice to save a copy, and anything that wanted it once usually wants it again.

member.summary: Starts a clip on a voice, holding a reference on the clip's shared buffer for as long as that voice can read from it.
member.remarks:
The native decoder reads straight out of that buffer on the audio thread, and the that loaded it is free to go in the meantime: an asset reimport disposes the cached instance, and a clip nothing holds a reference to is collected. Either one used to free the buffer out from under a sounding voice.
The new reference is taken before the old one is dropped, so replaying the same clip cannot pass through zero holders and free the buffer it is about to play from.

member.remarks: Called when the voice is torn down or pointed at something else, not when it is stopped. Stopping only clears a flag, and the audio thread can still be part way through a block, so the buffer has to outlive that. Anything holding a clip past its last sound is bounded by the voices a source owns, which is bounded by .

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.AudioSource.PlayOneShot(Prowl.Runtime.Resources.AudioClip,System.Single)
member.summary: Plays a clip on its own voice, without disturbing whatever this source is already playing. Overlapping calls layer instead of cutting each other off, which is what a one shot is for.
member.param: The clip to play.
Level for this voice alone, on top of the source's own volume.
member.remarks: Voices are pooled and share the source's sound group, so they inherit its volume, pitch and spatial settings and follow the object as it moves. Once are sounding at once the longest running one is taken over.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.AudioSource.AcquireOneShotVoice

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.AudioSource.TrimOneShotVoices
member.summary: Brings the pool down to the cap, quietest first: an idle voice costs nothing to take, so those go before anything still sounding, and only then the longest running, which is the order steals in.

member.summary: Destroys effects that were in the chain and are not in the list any more.

member.summary: The world space velocity the doppler shift is being driven from, in units per real second.
member.remarks: This used to difference the sound group's position against the previous position that Update had already overwritten with it, so it always answered roughly zero, and divided by a delta it never checked. It now reports the value Update actually handed the audio engine.

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.AudioSource.OutputTail
member.summary: Points this source's output at its mixer group, or at the engine endpoint when it has none. The group builds its own native node on demand, so this works whether the group has been used before or not.
Whatever runs last in this source is what feeds the bus: the effect node when it came up, the sound group itself otherwise. A failed effect node costs the effects, not the routing.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.AudioSource.RoutingIsStale
member.summary: True when what this source is attached to is no longer what it was told to feed, which is the one thing nothing else reports.
member.remarks: A bus rebuilds its node when the device changes, and its whole object is replaced when the mixer is reimported. Neither is something a source can see from the pointer it attached to.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.AudioSource.FollowGroup(Prowl.Runtime.Audio.AudioMixerGroup)
member.summary: Subscribes to the bus this source now feeds, and stops following the previous one.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.AudioSource.OnOutputGroupReleasing
member.summary: The bus this source feeds is tearing its node down. Let go now, while the call still lands on a node that exists, and let put this source on the rebuilt one.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.AudioSource.ClearRouting
member.summary: Stops following whatever bus this source was attached to.

The canvas discriminator keeps two equal-SortOrder canvases as contiguous layers instead of interleaving them.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshAgent.SamplePathPosition(Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshAreaMask,System.Single,Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshHit@)
member.summary:
How far along its current path the agent could get, without moving it: walks the path from where the agent stands and stops at , at the end of the path, or where the path first enters a polygon excludes.
True when the walk stopped short of . Two different things cause that, and the mask tells them apart: !hit.Mask.Overlaps(areaMask) means an excluded polygon blocked it, anything else means the path simply ran out. hit.Hit separately says the position is a real point on the path rather than one interpolated where the budget ran out, and hit.Distance is measured ALONG the path rather than to it.
Mid-hop across an off-mesh link the corridor already begins at the landing point, so the walk is measured from there rather than from where the agent hangs.
Areas are tested per POLYGON rather than per corner, so a path that only clips the corner of an excluded polygon still stops at it.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshLink
member.summary: Connects two navmesh positions that aren't walkably connected — a jump over a gap, a drop off a ledge, a ladder. Agents whose area mask includes traverse it as part of pathing; the crowd animates the hop and manual traversal is not supported. Links are BAKED data, kept beside the layers and re-injected whenever a tile is re-contoured, so carving and links coexist; with on this component rebuilds the tiles around its endpoints when it changes. Traversal cost comes from the area's cost, so price a link by giving it its own area. Enabled outside play too, because a bake gathers links from the registry only enabled links are in.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshModifier
member.summary: Changes how this GameObject (and, by default, its children) contributes to navmesh bakes: exclude it entirely, or override the area its geometry is stamped with. Resolved at geometry-collection time — the nearest modifier up the hierarchy wins, an object's own modifier always beats an inherited one, and a modifier with off covers only its own object. Changing a modifier does not rebake anything by itself; rebuild the surface (or the affected tiles) to apply. One modifier per GameObject: additional NavMeshModifier components on the same object are ignored.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshModifierVolume
member.summary: Stamps an area over a world region during navmesh bakes, independent of which objects the geometry came from — mark a danger zone, make a doorway expensive, or (with Not Walkable) erase walkability inside the box. The volume only re-marks surface that geometry produced; it never creates walkable surface. Applied during full bakes AND partial rebuilds whose tiles intersect it; like modifiers, changing a volume does not rebake anything by itself. When toggling or moving a volume at runtime, rebuild its ENTIRE footprint region — rebuilding a sub-region leaves the stamp half-applied in the untouched tiles.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshObstacle
member.summary:
Blocks agents while enabled — a parked vehicle, a dropped crate, a placed building.
on cuts a hole in the navmesh so pathfinding routes around it; the affected tiles rebuild over the following frames, and with the hole lifts while moving and re-applies once still for . Carving runs in the editor too, so placing a building shows the hole it will cut.
off is velocity-obstacle mode: the mesh is untouched and the obstacle joins each crowd as an immovable neighbour, so agents steer around it locally. Free to move, but paths are computed as if it weren't there, so an agent with no other route presses against it.
Either way the object's own geometry stays out of bakes — voxelizing it would freeze a hole where it happened to be standing.

members.member: The geometry setters and inspector edits both land here: a live carve is cut again at the new shape, and one that is not applied is left for the carve machinery to place.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshObstacle.UpdateBlockers
member.summary: Velocity-obstacle mode: keep one immovable agent per live crowd sitting on this obstacle, so every other agent's local avoidance treats it as a neighbour to steer around. Crowds appear lazily (when the first agent of a type registers), so membership is re-derived whenever the world's crowd count changes rather than only at enable.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshObstacle.RefreshBlockers(System.Single,System.Single)

The crowd's placement probe searches only a few units vertically (sized from ), so an obstacle floating well above the walkable surface — a tall Center offset, spawned mid-air — lands invalid.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshSurface
member.summary:
Bakes and registers a navmesh for one agent type. The baked result is a standalone asset, which the surface registers with the scene's on enable. Rebuilds run synchronously, in the background (), or per-tile for localized geometry changes ().
Registration is the whole of this component's lifecycle — there is no per-frame work — and it runs in the editor as well as in play: obstacles can only carve a live navmesh and the overlay draws one, so without it a scene's baked navmesh stays unregistered until something bakes again.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshSurface.MarkStaleBakedLinks
member.summary: Dirty the tiles of every link the registered navmesh disagrees with the scene about. A link catches itself up when it is missing, but one that was disabled, deactivated, deleted or rescoped since the bake never enables to take itself back out, and one edited while this surface was unregistered is already present under the same id. Both are found here by comparing definitions, and the drain rebuilds their tiles from the live set.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshSurface.RebuildCollectionBounds(Prowl.Vector.AABB)
member.summary:
World rect the collectors must cover for a rebuild of : the affected TILES plus the erosion border, because rebuilds rasterize whole tiles. Null when there is no grid to derive it from, meaning collect everything.
Public because the explicit-sources overload makes covering this rect the caller's job, and getting it wrong leaves holes rather than failing. Collectors clip terrain to the filter they are given, so the changed AABB alone is not conservative.

member.summary: Rebuild the tiles intersecting from caller-supplied geometry, for games whose world the collectors cannot see. Pass the bounds of the CHANGED geometry; the affected tile set derives from them plus the erosion border, and returns exactly the rect to collect against. Covering less is not a cheaper rebuild — partly covered tiles come back with holes. An empty source list is valid and empties the affected tiles.
member.param: Bounds of the changed geometry.
The geometry to bake the affected tiles from.

Area volumes applied to the rebuilt tiles. Null (the default) collects the scene's s over the affected region — note that collection walks the scene's active objects, so callers who chose explicit sources to avoid scene scans should pass an empty list (no volumes, no scan) or their own list.

member.summary: Voxelize the affected tiles on the thread pool, off the frame. The returned tiles are NOT yet live — apply them with from the main thread. Sequencing rules: do not run two rebuilds of overlapping regions concurrently, and do not interleave with a full rebake — the build reads the asset's grid anchoring and the apply assumes it is unchanged since dispatch.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshSurface.ApplyRebuiltTiles(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshTileRebuild})
member.summary:
Swap rebuilt tiles (from or ) into the live TileCache and mirror them into the asset. Main thread only.
A cache with carve work in flight cannot take a swap, and draining it inline costs milliseconds per queued tile under the write lock — so the swap is held until the frame the pump reports the cache settled, usually the next one. Anything queuing tile work sets that flag, a link rebuild included. A cache that never settles (an obstacle moving every frame re-queues as fast as the pump drains) gives up after a few passes and pays the drain. Use when the tiles must be live before the call returns.
False only when there is nothing to apply to; true means applied OR held. A held swap keeps the layer blobs handed to it, so do not recycle them until it lands.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshSurface.ApplyRebuiltTilesImmediately(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshTileRebuild})
member.remarks: Applies within the call instead of waiting for a settled frame: the swap quiesces pending obstacle work, replaces each tile's layers, refreshes every obstacle's touched-tile list (stale after a tile replacement bumps its salt), then rebuilds the new tiles with carves re-applied. Returns false, leaving the tiles as they were, when the cache cannot be quiesced. Called from a handler while a deferred swap is applying, it queues behind the swaps still waiting instead, since applying first would let them revert it.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.CharacterController
member.summary: A kinematic character that moves by sweeping its own shape through the world. It walks along the ground, slides along walls and ceilings, climbs steps, snaps down stairs and slopes, and rides whatever it stands on. It never becomes a rigidbody, so pushing things is left to the caller through .

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.CharacterController.Up
member.summary:
Which way is up for this controller, the opposite of the gravity the game applies. The shape stands along it, slopes, steps and ceilings are measured against it, and walking runs across it. Set it every frame for gravity that changes, such as walking round a planet.
Changing it turns the controller in place. A small turn pivots about the feet, so they stay planted on a curved world, and a large one about the middle of the shape, so a sudden flip turns the controller over where it is rather than swinging its head through the floor.

member.summary: Moves the controller by , sliding along whatever it meets. A move that does not rise while grounded walks along the ground, climbing steps and following slopes, and only falls once there is no ground within . Returns which sides were touched, holds what was touched.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.CharacterController.WalkAlongGround(Prowl.Vector.Float3,Prowl.Vector.Float3,Prowl.Vector.Float3)
member.summary: Walks a horizontal motion along the ground. Walkable surfaces met on the way become the new ground, anything steeper is climbed as a step if it is low enough and otherwise treated as an upright wall, so a slope too steep to walk or a ceiling sloping down to meet the floor is slid along rather than climbed or pressed into.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.CharacterController.TryStepUp(Prowl.Vector.Float3@,Prowl.Vector.Float3@,Prowl.Runtime.ShapeCastHit@,Prowl.Vector.Float3@)
member.summary: Lifts over something in the way: up by the step height, forward by what is left of the move, then down onto ground that can be stood on. Landing on the edge of the step is fine, the top face is what decides whether it is walkable.

member.summary: Drops onto walkable ground within the snap distance, which is what keeps the controller on stairs going down.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.CharacterController.FindGround(Prowl.Vector.Float3,System.Single,Prowl.Runtime.ShapeCastHit@,Prowl.Vector.Float3@,System.Single@)
member.summary: The ground below within reach. In the crease where walkable ground meets a steeper face, both are touched at once and the steep one can come first, so any standable surface met at about the same distance as the nearest counts. The drop is never past the nearest surface.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.CharacterController.SlideThroughAir(Prowl.Vector.Float3,Prowl.Vector.Float3)
member.summary: Moves freely, sliding along every surface met and along the crease where two meet. Coming down onto walkable ground ends the fall there and walks on with whatever horizontal motion is left.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.CharacterController.ClipToPlanes(Prowl.Vector.Float3,System.Int32)
member.summary: The part of a motion that runs along every plane met so far: along one plane if that keeps clear of the others, otherwise along the crease of two, otherwise nothing, which is a corner.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.CharacterController.StandableNormal(Prowl.Runtime.ShapeCastHit@,Prowl.Vector.Float3,Prowl.Vector.Float3@,Prowl.Vector.Float3)
member.summary: Whether a hit is something the controller can stand on, and the normal of the face it stands on. A rounded shape meets the edge of a face at an angle, so the face itself is found with a short ray just inside the contact. Already standing, the controller keeps standing on that face for as long as the bottom of its shape touches the edge. Coming down from the air it lands on the edge only with its middle over the face; with its middle outside it rolls off, the way a corner caught at the top of a jump that fell short should be.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.CharacterController.RidePlatforms(Prowl.Vector.Float3)
member.summary: Carries the controller along with whatever it stood on at the end of the last move. Standing on several moving things at once, such as the crease between two rollers, it moves by their average, which is what lets one hand it over to the next.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.CharacterController.Carry(Prowl.Vector.Float3,Prowl.Vector.Float3)
member.summary: Moves by a platform's motion, sliding along anything else in the way.

member.summary: Pushes the controller out of anything it is inside, deepest contact first, which lets a wedge settle over a few passes rather than being over corrected in one.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Collider.ComputeTransformVersion(Prowl.Vector.Transform)
member.summary:
A version that changes whenever this transform OR any ancestor up to changes. Transform.Version only tracks local edits, so a parent has to be walked for a child's world-space shapes to follow it.
Stopping at the attached body is what makes this usable for a moving rigidbody: the solver rewrites the body's own Transform every step, so including it would rebuild the shapes of every moving body every frame, while the offset between collider and body has not changed at all.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.DriveConstraint
member.summary: Pulls this body toward a target pose relative to the connected body, or to the world without one, with a spring and a damper on its position and another pair on its rotation, each with a limit on how hard it may push. The spring closes the gap to the target pose and the damper matches the target velocity, both solved inside the physics solver, so a drive stays stable however stiff it is set and whatever else is jointed to the body. The position drive acts between this body's origin and the target point on the connected body, so each body is pushed at that point and turned by the push as a real joint would be. Directions a body cannot move or turn in are left out of the drive.

member.summary: The position spring, in newtons per metre of gap.

member.summary: The position damper, in newtons per metre per second of speed off the target velocity.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.DriveConstraint.SpringDrive
member.summary: The solver side of . Each drive is a soft constraint: the spring and damper are folded into a bias and a softness, so the spring closes the error and the damper pulls toward the target velocity with exactly the force the pair would give, solved together with every other constraint on the bodies. The impulse is limited on each substep by the force times the substep's own time.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.PhysicsConstraint.IsLive(Jitter2.Dynamics.Constraints.Constraint)
member.summary:
Whether a constraint is live enough to read or write its properties.
A non-null check is not sufficient. Jitter's constraint properties are views onto unmanaged memory, and removing a body automatically removes its constraints while this component still holds the managed object. Disabling a rigidbody that has a joint on it is enough to get there, and writing through an invalid constraint would access unavailable state.

member.summary: Provides physics collision for terrain using heightmap-based collision detection. Samples height data directly from the TerrainData asset (no separate cache).

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.TerrainCollider.LocalToWorld
member.summary:
The grid placement, refreshed from the transform once per frame rather than read per query. The broad phase samples this from Jitter's worker threads, and Transform's cached world matrix is not safe to touch concurrently; caching also keeps the per-sample height lookup off it entirely.
The grid is defined in terrain-local space, so position, rotation and scale all live in these matrices rather than being baked into the samples. That is what lets terrain be turned to any orientation and still collide correctly.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.TriggerVolume
member.summary:
A non-solid sensor volume. It does not collide with or push anything; instead it queries the physics world each fixed step for overlapping rigidbodies and raises enter/stay/exit events. Use it for pickups, checkpoints, damage zones, detectors, and similar gameplay triggers.
Only bodies that can be identified (a ) are reported. Static geometry shares a per-layer body and has no component to hand back, so it is ignored. s have no body, so they are tested directly and reported through the separate character callbacks.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.WheelCollider
member.summary:
A raycast-vehicle wheel. Ground contact is a grid of downward rays across the wheel face. Each ray finds the surface below it, and the wheel's contact with that surface is solved exactly for its round profile, so it sits precisely on slopes and still rides over bumps and kerbs between rays. Suspension is a spring and damper tuned from a natural frequency, and grip follows a friction curve on slip ratio and slip angle, solved together with the wheel's spin so it stays stable for any mass and holds still on slopes and moving platforms.
The wheel applies forces to the nearest enabled above it; it does not add a collision shape of its own. Place the wheel GameObject so its position marks the top of the suspension travel; the wheel hangs below along -up. Positive turns toward the wheel's right.

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.WheelCollider.SteerAngle
member.summary: Steering angle in radians about the suspension axis, positive toward the wheel's right. Set by a controller.

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.WheelCollider.MotorTorque
member.summary: Drive torque in N m applied to the wheel spin. Set by a controller each frame.

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.WheelCollider.BrakeTorque
member.summary: Brake torque in N m opposing the wheel spin. Set by a controller each frame. Negative values count as zero.

member.summary: Wheel tilt in degrees about the forward axis, mirrored per side so one value suits both. Positive leans the tops inward.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.Terrain.TerrainMeshDetailRenderer
member.summary:
Scatters mesh detail prototypes across the terrain, on the CPU.
Textured details are placed in the vertex shader by , but a mesh prototype renders with its own user-authored materials, which know nothing about procedural placement. Those get instances built here instead, one set around each camera that draws the terrain, which views of that camera then frustum cull on the render thread.
A set covers the whole draw distance around its camera. It is built with a margin of slack and only rebuilt once the camera has spent it, and placement is seeded from the world cell index, so a rebuild puts every instance back exactly where it was.

member.summary: Instances one prototype may place at once, so a solid paint cannot stall a frame.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.TextMeshComponent
member.summary:
Draws text as a mesh in arbitrary 3D world space, independent of any . The glyph geometry is generated once by Scribe (shared atlas via ), baked into a cached , and drawn through the Default/DefaultTextMesh SDF shader - so it stays crisp at any distance without the per-frame cost of a canvas.
The text is anchored around the transform origin (see ), so a centered anchor puts the middle of the text on the object's position. To make a camera-facing nameplate, rotate the transform to face the camera yourself (billboard); nothing here forces an orientation.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.UI.EventSystem
member.summary: Drives GameObject-UI input. A scene needs exactly one enabled for its es to receive pointer and keyboard events. Each frame it hit-tests the pointer against the scene's canvases (via ) and dispatches enter/exit, press, drag, click, scroll, submit/cancel and selection events to the components under it.
member.remarks: This is entirely game-space: it ticks from (play mode only) and nothing in the engine loop drives it. A has no dependency on it - delete this component and canvases still render, they just stop receiving input - so you can drop in your own event system. Access the active one through .

Volumetric clouds over the whole scene, with optional flat cloud layers above or below them.
The cloud layer is ray marched through the view at a reduced resolution, taking its density from a coverage map around the camera and eroding its edges with 3D noise, lit from a sun map drawn once a frame or by marching a few steps toward the sun. member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Debug.EnsureMainThread(System.String)
member.summary:
Reports when a main-thread-only API is called from somewhere else, and says whether it was. Deduplicated per caller, because an offending call site usually repeats every frame.
The point is to fail where the rule was broken. Touching scene or engine state off-thread usually surfaces as a corrupted read or a crash somewhere unrelated, long after the call that caused it. Callers that can bail should act on the result; the rest at least get a name.
Always true before a is installed (tests, tools, early startup), since there is no engine thread to be off.
member.param: Defaults to the calling member.
member.returns: True when the caller is on the main thread.

Where each frame's main-thread time goes, by category, over the last frames.
using FrameStatScope stats = FrameStats.Physics.Scope(); // built-in category, to the end of the method using (FrameStats.Scope("AI")) UpdateAgents(); // your own, created on first use using (FrameStats.Scope("AI/Paths")) FindPaths(); // grouped under AI in viewers float avg = FrameStats.Render.GetStats(60).Avg; // ms per frame, last 60 frames
Nested scopes count only their own time, so a frame's categories add up to its length, with unscoped time in and GC pauses in . Scopes off the main thread record nothing.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.EngineObject.Destroy
member.summary:
Queues this object to be disposed at the end of the frame, once every callback has finished. It stays fully usable until then, so anything still holding it this frame keeps working, and teardown never lands in the middle of an Update, a render or a physics callback.

member.summary:
Called each frame right before Paper.BeginFrame. Sets Paper's logical resolution to the window's logical size (OS points) and DisplayFramebufferScale to . Quill's TransformPoint multiplies every vertex by DisplayFramebufferScale, so vertices span [0, winSize × cs] = [0, fbSize], exactly matching the orthographic projection set up by .
A widget declared Width(100) occupies 100 logical points = 100 physical pixels at 1× DPI and 200 physical pixels at 2× (Retina) DPI the same physical size on screen regardless of display density, with higher pixel quality on HiDPI displays.

member.summary:
Removes a specific component from the GameObject.
A component the prefab provides is not the instance's to remove while the editor is the thing holding it: nothing records that it went, so the next time the instance is brought back into line with its prefab it would simply reappear. The editor's own remove offers to break the connection first and then comes back here. In play mode and in a player nothing refreshes an instance, so nothing stands in the way there.
member.param: The component instance to remove.

Marks a freshly built tree as an instance of the prefab it came from, recording which prefab object each one is. Stops at objects that already belong to a different prefab, which are nested instances with their own link.
The tree still wears the prefab's own identifiers at this point, so each object is holding the answer already: it notes down what it came in as and is given a fresh identity of its own. member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.SceneCallbacks
member.summary: Which optional callbacks a component actually overrides. Resolved once per instance and cached on it, so neither the per-frame loops nor the physics events pay a type lookup.

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.SceneCallbacks.AnyFrame
member.summary: Everything the per-frame loops dispatch. A component with none of these is never registered.

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.SceneCallbacks.Resolved
member.summary: Set once this instance's set has been worked out. The unresolved state is deliberately the default value rather than a sentinel: a component's fields can arrive zeroed after a hot reload without the engine assembly's IL being available to replay an initializer, and a sentinel that depended on that would silently decay into "overrides nothing".

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.SceneDispatcher
member.summary: The scene's single dispatch point for component callbacks: the per-frame loops (Start, Update, LateUpdate, FixedUpdate, DrawGizmos, OnGui) and the sparse physics events (collision and trigger). Both used to be separate types doing the same job at different granularities, and the physics half paid a type lookup per component per event, which is the wrong cost to carry on a contact callback.
member.remarks:
Three things keep this cheap. A component's callback set is resolved once and cached on the instance, so a dispatch test is a field read and a mask AND rather than a dictionary probe. Registration is a dense array with swap-back removal, so enabling or destroying a component is constant time instead of a scan per channel. And a channel's execution-ordered array is rebuilt at most once per frame no matter how many components joined or left, rather than re-sorted on every membership change.
Across a hot reload the walk migrates the component references in place, then drops every derived answer so membership and ordering are re-derived from the new types: a component that newly overrides a callback starts dispatching, and one that dropped it stops.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.SceneDispatcher.CallbacksOf(Prowl.Runtime.Component)
member.summary: The component's callback set, resolved from its type the first time it is asked for and cached on the instance. The cache field is opted out of hot reload, so a replaced instance arrives unresolved and picks up whatever its new type overrides.

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.SceneDispatcher.CollisionListeners
member.summary: Enabled components that listen for a collision event. Physics tracks no contacts while there are none.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.SceneDispatcher.Register(Prowl.Runtime.Component)
member.summary: Starts dispatching a component's per-frame callbacks. Called whenever it becomes enabled in an active scene; the per-tick gameplay gate decides whether they actually run.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.SceneDispatcher.Unregister(Prowl.Runtime.Component)
member.summary: Stops dispatching a component's per-frame callbacks. Constant time.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.SceneDispatcher.Reset
member.summary: Drops every derived answer: registration, channel membership, and each component's cached callback set and ordering. The caller re-registers from the live scene afterwards.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.SceneDispatcher.Channel
member.summary: The components subscribed to one callback, in execution order. Rebuilt lazily, so a frame that enables a thousand components pays one rebuild rather than a thousand re-sorts, and iterating the rebuilt array keeps a loop safe against a callback enabling or disabling something mid-dispatch.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.SceneDispatcher.DispatchOrder
member.summary: Execution order first, then registration order. Comparing two cached ints keeps the sort off the reflection path entirely, and the sequence tie-break makes the result independent of array position, which is what lets registration use swap-back removal.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.DefaultInputHandler.BeginFrame
member.summary: Drops the previous frame's typed characters, before DoEvents appends this frame's. Clearing here rather than in LateUpdate is what lets them survive the whole frame - the editor pumps the Game View's Paper during Render, which is after LateUpdate, so a clear there dropped every character before that Paper could see one.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.Win32Clipboard
member.summary: Reads the Windows clipboard directly, so it is always closed again.
member.remarks: GLFW reports clipboard failures through its error callback, which Silk raises as a managed exception from inside native code. Unwinding out of the callback skips the CloseClipboard that follows it, leaving the clipboard open and owned by this process and locking every other application out of it. So we handle reading clipboard manually to circumvent that issue.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshAreas
member.summary:
The project-wide navigation area table: up to 32 named areas with per-area path costs, addressed by index and combined into 32-bit masks. Area 0 is Walkable, 1 is Not Walkable, 2 is Jump; 3..31 are user-defined.
Detour stores area i as i + 1, because its 0 is the null area meaning "not part of the navmesh". / are the only places that offset is applied — never hand-roll it. Bake-side conversions go through ProwlInputGeomProvider.DetourAreaFor, which additionally maps to the null area; calling on a source area instead silently resurrects traversable "Not Walkable" polys.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshBuilder
member.summary: Builds a from collected geometry. Pure CPU work over an already-flattened triangle soup — no Transform or GameObject access — so it is safe to run on a background thread once the sources have been collected on the main thread. Navmeshes are always built tiled so they can be partially rebuilt later (see NavMeshSurface.RebuildTiles).
Build a complete navmesh from geometry sources. Returns null when nothing walkable was produced (no geometry, all down-facing, cancelled) — never an empty NavMeshData.
member.param: Agent envelope + voxelization parameters. Snapshotted into the result.
Collected geometry. Vertices are transformed by each source's matrix during flattening.
Area for sources that don't specify one (see ).
Worker threads for tile building. 0 or 1 builds single-threaded (deterministic tile order).
Cancels between tiles; a cancelled build returns null.
Explicit XZ extent for the tile grid. Size the grid from this rather than from the geometry so RebuildTiles can add tiles anywhere inside it later. The vertical range still unions with the geometry.
Convex area volumes stamped over the rasterized geometry. They never create walkable surface; a Not Walkable volume erases it.
Off-mesh connections, placed in the tile containing their start point and re-injected as each tile is contoured — runtime tiles rebuild from geometry-only layers.

member.summary:
Rebuild the compressed layers of the tiles intersecting .. against fresh geometry, keeping the original bake's tile grid. A region entirely outside the baked bounds is a no-op, since growing the bounds needs a full rebuild. Returns one entry per affected tile; an empty layer list means the tile is now empty. Apply with , which refreshes obstacle state so existing carves re-apply to the regenerated tiles.
XZ anchors to the ORIGINAL bake bounds, never the current geometry, or tile (0,0) shifts and every tile misaligns against the live navmesh. Y follows the current geometry because Recast clips spans to the heightfield's vertical range.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshBuilder.AddVolumes(Prowl.Runtime.ProwlInputGeomProvider,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshAreaVolume})
member.summary: Hand area volumes to the provider as Recast convex volumes; the stock pipeline applies them to the compact heightfield after rasterization (RcBuilder.Build → MarkConvexPolyArea), which only re-marks spans geometry produced — Not Walkable maps to the null area and erases them.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshBuilder.ResolveTileSize(Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshBuildSettings)
member.summary:
Pin the resolved tile size into so the bake, the serialized asset, its TileCache, and later rebuilds all agree on one value.
A compressed layer header stores tile dimensions as BYTES: a tile wider than voxels wraps and decompresses as an empty layer, so the bake "succeeds" with no polygons. clamps to prevent that; this just warns when the clamp actually moved the user's value.

member.summary: Off-mesh links. Tiles are rebuilt from geometry-only layers whenever an obstacle carves or a region regenerates — anything baked into them is regenerated away — so links live here and are re-injected on every tile build. Kept in step with the live s by .

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshData.ResolveCapacity
member.summary:
The tile and polygon capacities this asset instantiates with. Every vertical layer occupies its own navmesh tile slot, and multi-layer tiles (overlapping floors, bridges) are the point of the layer set, so the budget must exceed the baked layer count rather than merely reach it: a rebuild that stacks a new layer has to land somewhere. An asset whose layers already fill its baked budget (one baked before the budget carried the layer factor, or a scene that stacks deeper than the bake allowed for) is re-sized from its actual layer count, splitting the shared id bits with the same arithmetic the bake used.
The tile cache is created with the same tile count, so a layer the cache accepts always has somewhere to land. Detour drops tiles past capacity through a status the cache discards, so the two must never disagree.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshData.MeshTiles(Prowl.Recast.Detour.TileCache.DtTileCache,System.Collections.Generic.List{System.Int64})
member.summary:
Mesh every layer. This is the whole cost of registering a navmesh — 0.65–1.5 ms per tile, on the main thread inside OnEnable — so it fans out: the build half of a tile touches no navmesh state, and only the commit does. Safe here and nowhere else, because the mesh is not published until this returns, so no query can be running and nothing can carve.
Commits run serially in ref order, which is what makes the result identical to a serial bake: tile linking follows the order tiles are added. Measured on a 256-tile bake: 85 ms against 500 ms, for 9% more allocation (a neighbour-layer cache per worker instead of one).

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshGeometryCollector.CollectTerrain(Prowl.Runtime.Terrain.TerrainComponent,System.Single,System.Int32,System.Collections.Generic.List{Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshGeometrySource},System.Nullable{Prowl.Vector.AABB})
member.summary:
Collect a terrain as a decimated height grid. Samples are spaced no finer than the bake voxel size — Recast re-voxelizes at that resolution anyway, so finer triangles are pure waste (a 1k heightmap would otherwise contribute ~2M triangles). Holes are skipped, and a bounds filter clips the sampled range rather than only rejecting the terrain outright, so a partial rebuild pays for its own tiles instead of the whole heightmap.
Heights come from in terrain-local space, placed by the object's transform exactly as places the physics heightfield — so a moved, rotated or scaled terrain walks where it's drawn and where it collides. Reading the asset (not the collider) is also what lets a bake with the editor open see terrain at all.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshGeometryCollector.SampleFloor(System.Single,System.Single,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Heightmap index bracketing a terrain-local coordinate, snapped outwards onto the stride grid an unclipped collect samples. The snap is what keeps a clipped source decimating to the same surface: sampling the same span at a shifted phase gives different heights, and a rebuilt tile would then step away from a neighbour that was not rebuilt. One sample of slack covers the quads straddling the clip edge.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.NavMeshWorld
member.summary:
Per-scene navigation state: the registered navmeshes, the query API over them, and (once agents register) the crowd simulation. Owned by the same way physics state is owned by .
Queries are thread-safe: each takes a pooled Detour query under a read lock, so gameplay code may path-find from worker threads. Tile mutations take the write lock and invalidate pooled queries.

Raised when queued work finishes and the navmesh is stable again. A carve spans several frames, and anything expensive — re-pathing a crowd, rebuilding a cached triangulation — wants to run once at the end rather than on each of them.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.PhysicsWorld
member.summary:
A scene's physics simulation and the queries against it.
Threading: every member here is main-thread only, and queries additionally must not overlap each other. Jitter's own read paths are thread-safe, so this is Prowl's restriction rather than Jitter's: the query layer reuses scratch buffers, and a query first pushes pending Transform edits into their bodies. Breaking either rule is reported rather than silently returning wrong results. If you need a query from a job, marshal it back.

member.summary:
Bake (or fetch the cached) physics representation of a mesh. The bake is stored directly on the instance (), so its lifetime is tied to the mesh rather than a separate global cache. The result is shared by every collider that uses the mesh, so the bake happens once instead of per MeshCollider instance, and is rebuilt automatically when the mesh's changes.

member.summary: Pushes any changed Transforms into their physics bodies and collider shapes (transform -> body). Runs automatically before each simulation step when is on. Call it manually to make Transform edits visible to queries, which never sync on their own.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.PhysicsWorld.RefreshColliders

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.PhysicsWorld.EnhancedDeterminism
member.summary: When true, uses Jitter2's deterministic island-based solver instead of the regular parallel solver. Slower but produces identical results across runs required for networked physics, replays, or lockstep simulation.

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.PhysicsWorld.ThreadModel
member.summary: Thread model for the physics step. Persistent keeps worker threads alive between steps (lower latency, higher idle CPU). Regular spins them up per step (higher latency, lower idle CPU).

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.PhysicsWorld.EnableAuxiliaryContactPoints
member.summary: Generates extra contact points along the perimeter of contact patches for improved stability on flat surfaces. Default true. Disable for slight perf gain at the cost of stability.

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.PhysicsWorld.PersistentContactManifold
member.summary: Persists contact manifolds across frames (warm-starts the solver). Default true. Disable for slight memory savings; significantly hurts stack stability if turned off.

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.PhysicsWorld.SpeculativeRelaxationFactor
member.summary: Damping factor (0..1) applied to speculative contact correction. Lower = softer prediction. Default 0.9.

member.summary: Rejects query inputs that would take NaN or infinity into the solver. Jitter's support maps use Math.Sign on the search direction, which throws outright on NaN, so a single poisoned caller would otherwise crash the frame from deep inside the narrow phase. Reporting no hit and naming the query gives the caller something to act on instead.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.TerrainCollisionFilter.RegisterTriangleContact(Jitter2.Collision.Shapes.RigidBodyShape,Jitter2.Dynamics.RigidBodyData@,Prowl.Runtime.CollisionTriangle@,System.UInt64)
member.summary: Registers a contact against one terrain triangle. A degenerate cell (repeated corners, or a terrain whose data has not sized itself yet) has a zero-area cross product, and normalising that yields NaN rather than zero - feeding it to the solver poisons every body it touches.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.TerrainCollisionFilter.ProcessTerrainCollision(Jitter2.Collision.Shapes.RigidBodyShape)
member.summary:
Processes collision between a rigidbody shape and the terrain.
Runs on Jitter's broad-phase worker threads, and reads the heightmap and hole mask straight out of the TerrainData. Sculpting is main-thread and happens between steps, so the two never overlap; editing terrain from inside a subscriber would be the one way to race this, and is not something to do.
Cells are picked in terrain-local space, where the grid is axis-aligned however the terrain is rotated, and each candidate triangle is then taken back out to world space so the narrow phase can meet the body where it lives.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.ITerrainHeightProvider
member.summary:
Supplies the height grid and where it sits in the world.
The grid itself is defined in terrain-local space: cell (x,z) sits at (x, height, z) * CellSize with no rotation, scale or offset baked in. carries all of that, which is what lets terrain be rotated arbitrarily - queries are brought into local space, walked on the axis-aligned grid there, and their results taken back out.

member.returns: True if the coordinates are valid and height was retrieved.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.ITerrainHeightProvider.TryGetCellRange(Jitter2.LinearMath.JBoundingBox@,System.Int32@,System.Int32@,System.Int32@,System.Int32@)
member.summary:
The range of cells a world-space bounding box could touch, clamped to the grid. Upper bounds are exclusive, so callers iterate x < maxX.
The box is brought into local space corner by corner and re-bounded there, because a rotated terrain turns an axis-aligned world box into an oriented one. Re-bounding is conservative, which is what a broad-phase range has to be.
member.returns: False when the box cannot touch the grid at all.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.Rendering.LightProbeVolume
member.summary: Runtime light-probe sampler. Built from a baked set of probe positions + SH and a precomputed tetrahedralization (tetra vertex indices + per-face neighbour links, produced by the editor's bake). locates the tetrahedron containing a world position, then barycentric-blends the four corner probes' SH; points outside the hull fall back to a nearby blend.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Rendering.LightProbeVolume.ComputeBarycentric(System.Int32,Prowl.Vector.Float3,System.Single@,System.Single@,System.Single@,System.Single@)
member.summary: Barycentric coords of in tetra (b0 = corner 0, etc.). Returns false only when the tetrahedron is degenerate (near-zero volume) - the grid tetrahedralization can emit zero-volume slivers on the real positions - so the caller skips it. The coordinates are output even when is outside the tet (some negative), so the caller can both test containment and find the nearest boundary tet for extrapolation.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.Rendering.VolumetricCloudsFeature
member.summary:
Draws a scene's over its opaques and sky, under the transparents, as a feature of the scene's world.
Each view draws a coverage map around its camera holding how much cloud there is at every point of the ground plane, and a sun map holding how much cloud the sunlight crosses. The cloud layer and the flat layers are marched front to back at a reduced resolution, a quarter of its pixels a frame with temporal upscaling, and scaled up over the scene with depth aware weights so the clouds stay behind geometry edges.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Resources.AudioClip.#ctor(System.Byte[],System.Boolean)
member.summary: Creates a new AudioClip instance which gets its data from memory. The data must be in an encoded format.
member.param: Must be encoded audio data (either WAV/MP3/FLAC/OGG)

Give this clip a buffer of its own instead of sharing one with every other clip holding the same bytes. Sharing is the default because it is what stops ten prefabs referencing one sound from holding ten copies of it, and nothing writes to the buffer once it is loaded.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Resources.AudioClip.AcquireHandle(System.Byte[],System.Boolean)
member.summary: Points this clip at a buffer holding and takes a reference on it, letting go of whatever it held before. The byte array is the authority on the size, so a stored length that disagrees with the stored bytes can't make playback read past the allocation.
member.remarks: A shared buffer is keyed on a hash of the bytes, so two clips holding the same audio hold one allocation. A unique one is keyed on a counter from a space content hashes cannot reach, which is what makes it actually unique: keyed on the identity hash of the array, as it was, two clips could be handed the same key and share a buffer neither of them expected to share.

How many channels the samples are interleaved across.
Sample rate of the samples in hertz.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Resources.AudioClip.WriteWave(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Single},System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Wraps interleaved float samples in a minimal WAVE container.
member.param: Interleaved float samples.
Number of interleaved channels.
Samples per second per channel.

Store as 16 bit PCM rather than 32 bit float, halving the size for a noise floor no game source material gets near. Float keeps a procedurally built clip bit exact through a round trip, which is why it is the default.
member.remarks: Written straight into the one array that is returned. A stream to build it in and a copy out of that stream meant three copies of a decoded clip alive at once during an import, which for a long track is hundreds of megabytes, most of it on the large object heap.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Resources.AudioClip.ContentHash(System.Byte[])
member.summary: The key a shared buffer holding is held under.
member.remarks:
A digest rather than something rolled by hand, because of what a collision costs here: two clips landing on one key share a buffer, so one plays the other's audio, and the reference count frees it while the other is still reading. Neither symptom points anywhere near a hash function. This runs once per clip when it is loaded, and the hardware does it faster than a byte at a time loop could.
The top bit is dropped because keys clips that asked not to share above it.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.Resources.ComputeShader
member.summary:
GLSL that runs on the GPU outside of drawing. A .compute file declares its entry points with #pragma kernel Name X Y Z, the thread group size (Y and Z default to 1), and each one is a plain void Name() function reading gl_GlobalInvocationID and friends. Storage blocks and images need no binding layout, Graphite assigns them and binds by name.
Values set with and the like apply to every kernel, buffers and textures are set per kernel. A dispatch runs at once, ahead of anything submitted later, so a buffer read afterwards sees its results. For work inside the frame, write a Graphite RenderFeature or RenderProvider instead.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.Resources.MeshGeometry
member.summary:
Converts between and , so the geometry operators can work on engine meshes.
Mesh vertices that share a position become one geometry vertex, and everything a mesh vertex carries (normal, tangent, UVs, color, skinning, blend shape offsets) is kept per corner on the loops. Split vertices therefore show up as loops at one vertex with different values, which is what the operators treat as seams, so both sides of a split stay joined. Each face records its submesh.
A triangle that reuses corners another triangle already took, like the back of a double sided card, goes onto its own copy of those vertices so each side stays a clean surface. A triangle whose corners share a position gets vertices of its own and is kept as it is.
Skinning comes back in a canonical slot order: sorted by bone, unused slots on bone 0.

member.summary: One blend shape frame's attribute names, resolved once rather than per corner.

member.summary: Builds geometry from a triangle mesh. Throws for a submesh with triangles in another topology.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.Resources.MeshGeometry.ToMesh(Prowl.Vector.Geometry.GeometryData,Prowl.Runtime.Resources.Mesh)
member.summary: Builds a mesh from geometry. One mesh vertex is made per distinct corner of each geometry vertex. supplies what geometry does not carry: name, bind poses, bone names, blend shape names and frame weights, whether colors were bytes, and the submesh count, so a submesh that lost every triangle still keeps its slot and the material order holds. member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.MeshFeatures.Generation.SDFGenerator
member.summary:
CPU generator for the signed distance field stored in , negative inside.
Exact distances are found only near the surface, where each triangle visits the voxels around it. Every other voxel takes the closest triangle of a neighbour in sweeps along each axis and measures the exact distance to it, so the cost grows with the voxels and the triangles rather than their product.
A voxel is inside when rays along at least two of the three axes cross the surface an odd number of times before reaching it. Counting crossings ignores which way a triangle faces, so flipped and one sided triangles change nothing, and a hole or a stray plane only misleads the axis it lines up with, which the other two outvote.

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.MeshFeatures.Generation.SDFGenerator.Options.MaxResolution
member.summary: Most voxels along any axis, padding included. Large meshes use larger voxels to stay within it.

member.summary: Fewest voxels along the longest axis, padding included.

member.summary: Async helpers for game code: moving between the main thread and worker threads, and waiting on frames and game time.

member.summary: Cancelled when the session the calling code belongs to ends: play mode stopping, scripts reloading or the game quitting. member.summary: Waits for real time, ignoring time scale and pausing.

member.summary: Queues work for the main thread without waiting for it. Dropped if the session that started the work ends first. Runs at once when no loop is running.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.GameTask.Run(System.Action)
member.summary: Runs work on the main thread and blocks until it finishes, rethrowing what it threw. Runs at once when called on the main thread or when no loop is running, and carries over a session ending, since the caller is waiting. Throws if the loop stops first. Never call it from a thread the main thread is waiting on.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext
member.summary: Sends async continuations back to the main thread, so await in game code resumes where the scene actually lives.
member.remarks:
Without a synchronization context everything after an await resumes on a thread pool thread, and ordinary game code ends up touching the scene from the wrong thread, which only sometimes crashes. Installing one makes await behave the way the code reads.
Each context is one session. The editor ends a session when play starts or stops and when scripts reload: the session token is cancelled and every continuation still waiting on it is dropped, so a method that awaited during play never resumes against the edit scene or runs code that was reloaded. A dropped method simply stops, so its finally blocks do not run. Work that must clean up watches instead.
Gameplay work stays tied to its session across threads: anything started from a scene callback or from main thread queued work carries the session with its execution context, so a worker that hops back with await GameTask.MainThread() after its session ended is dropped too. Everything else, such as editor code, long lived threads and work that suppresses execution context flow, follows the current session. Blocking calls are the exception and carry over, since a thread is waiting on them.

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext.Current
member.summary: The context the engine installed, or null when no loop is running.

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext.Origin
member.summary: The session the calling code belongs to: the current one on the main thread, and on a worker the one that started the gameplay work it is running, falling back to the current one. After it is the stopped session, so anything asking for the main thread is refused. Null when no loop is running.

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext.Live
member.summary: The installed context, or the stopped one while shutdown finishes.

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.Tasks.MainThreadContext.IsMainThread
member.summary: Whether the caller is on the thread the engine pumps.

member.summary: Whether the caller is on the engine's thread, for main thread only APIs to check themselves. True when no context has been installed (tests, tools, early startup), since there is no engine thread to be off yet and refusing to run would be worse than the race being guarded against.

member.summary: Whether this session has ended.

member.summary: Completes at the start of the next , or is cancelled if the session ends first.

member.summary: Completes at the start of the first where returns true, checked on the main thread once per frame. Cancelled if the session ends first, so it never hangs.

member.summary: Installs a context bound to the calling thread, which must be the one running the loop. Replaces any installed one the way does.

member.summary: Ends the current session and starts a new one on the same thread. Must be called on the main thread. Called from inside async code, the thread's synchronization context is put back by the runtime when that code returns, so the next points it at the new session again.

member.summary: Ends the session for good, for when the loop stops. Blocked calls still queued run here. Until the ownership checks stay armed and any request for the main thread is refused, so a worker cannot run main thread work alongside the shutdown.

member.summary: Stops the loop if it is still running and removes it, so every thread counts as the main thread again.

member.summary: Marks the code run inside the scope as gameplay work of the current session, so what it starts on other threads stays tied to that session. Used around the scene callbacks and the main thread queue.

member.summary: Lets the calling flow follow the current session from here on, for editor code that deliberately outlives the gameplay session it may have been started in.

member.summary: Runs everything queued for the main thread. Called once per frame by the game loop.
member.remarks: Drains a snapshot of what was already waiting rather than looping until empty, so a continuation that queues more work cannot keep the pump running and stall the frame.

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.Time.FixedAccumulator
member.summary:
How far the frame being drawn sits past the last fixed step, in seconds - the fixed loop leaves this holding whatever part of the frame its steps did not consume, so it is always under by the time the scene's Update runs.
This is the alpha physics interpolation has to render at. Counting time since the last step with a per-frame accumulator instead does not work: the step that resets such a counter happens partway through a frame, and the whole of that frame's delta then gets added on top of time the step already consumed, which reads back a pose the body has not reached yet. Owned by the game loop - read it, do not write it.

member.summary:
A MultiValueDictionary can be viewed as a that allows multiple values for any given unique key. While the MultiValueDictionary API is mostly the same as that of a regular , there is a distinction in that getting the value for a key returns a of values rather than a single value associated with that key. Additionally, there is functionality to allow adding or removing more than a single value at once.
The MultiValueDictionary can also be viewed as a IReadOnlyDictionary<TKey,IReadOnlyCollection<TValue>t> where the is abstracted from the view of the programmer.
For a read-only MultiValueDictionary, see .

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.RuntimeUtils.ResolveType(System.String)
member.summary: Resolves a type from an assembly-qualified name across ALL loaded assembly load contexts, including the collectible context user scripts are loaded into. can only bind names into the default context by CLR rule, so it returns null for any type declared in a user assembly - which is why persisted type names (asset entries, and anything else round-tripped through ) need this instead.
member.remarks: Unlike , this honors the assembly recorded in the name and never falls back to a loose simple-name match, so it cannot return the wrong type when two assemblies declare types that share a name. Assemblies are matched on simple name only: a script assembly keeps its name but gets a fresh version and load context on every hot-reload, so matching full identity would miss it. Returns null rather than throwing for malformed or unloadable names.

member.name: T:Prowl.Runtime.SceneReferenceResolver
member.summary:
Echo external-reference resolver for scene objects. The objects passed to the constructor - the copy selection, or the tree being written to an asset - serialize by value; every other GameObject / Component / Transform reference is linked by its persistence id and resolved back against the current scene, so the copy keeps its references to the rest of the scene instead of deep-cloning them into orphans. References that can't be resolved (different scene, deleted object) become null.
Shared across the flows that serialize part of a scene: component copy/paste, GameObject duplication, and prefab creation/apply. Each passes the roots it is serializing by value, and everything outside that set is linked.

member.name: F:Prowl.Runtime.SceneReferenceResolver.None
member.summary: Links nothing and resolves nothing, for reading content that must not bind to the scene at all - a prefab asset, which cannot legally reference scene objects. Echo only recognises a reference stub while a resolver is present, so this is what turns an external reference into null instead of an empty object rebuilt from the stub. Deserialization only: serializing with it would deep-copy every reference rather than link it.

member.name: M:Prowl.Runtime.SceneReferenceResolver.#ctor(System.Object[])
member.param: The objects being serialized by value. Anything they reference that isn't in this set is linked by id instead of cloned. Pass nothing when only deserializing (paste), since the key side is never consulted then.

member.name: P:Prowl.Runtime.SceneReferenceResolver.ResolveIn
member.summary: Which scene a link resolves against. Null means the open one, which is right for everything the user does directly. A caller working on a scene that is not open - a build reading one off disk - has to say so, or its references resolve against whatever scene happens to be open and bind to the wrong objects or to nothing.
